# Spring Boot Web Application using jlink and Multi-Architecture Image Builds

This runbook combines two focused container image techniques:

- creating a custom Java runtime with `jlink`;
- publishing one application image reference that can resolve to different
  platform-specific image manifests.

It is intentionally a composition example. You can read and run it on its own,
but it does not repeat the full explanation from the deeper examples:

- [Spring Boot Web Application using Slim Java runtime (JRE)](../jlink-slim-image-spring-boot/README.md)
  explains module selection and the mechanics of building a smaller runtime
  image with `jlink`.
- [Spring Boot Web Application using Multi-Architecture Image Builds](../multi-architecture-image-builds-spring-boot/README.md)
  explains OCI image indexes, platform-specific manifests, and local
  multi-platform archive inspection in more detail.

The additional lesson here is the interaction between those two ideas. A `jlink`
runtime is not architecture-neutral. When a multi-platform build runs `jlink`,
the custom runtime must be created separately for each requested platform. The
`linux/amd64` image variant must contain an `amd64` runtime, and the
`linux/arm64` image variant must contain an `arm64` runtime.

This is a focused example, not a complete Java-in-containers reference
architecture. It deliberately leaves out concerns such as non-root runtime
users, image signing, vulnerability scanning, observability, SBOM generation,
Spring Boot layer extraction, CDS archives, Leyden AOT caches, and
deployment-specific hardening. For a more holistic Spring Boot container example
that combines several workshop concerns, see
[all-in-one-spring-boot](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md).

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- Either [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with Buildx, or
  [Podman](https://podman.io/) with manifest support.

- [Skopeo](https://github.com/containers/skopeo).

- `curl`, used to call the Spring Boot endpoint.

- `jq`, used to inspect OCI JSON documents.

- `tree`, used to inspect generated directories in the walkthrough.

Additional setup inputs:

- [Oracle Account](https://profile.oracle.com/myprofile/account/create-account.jspx)
  to access [Oracle Container Registry](https://container-registry.oracle.com/)

- An Oracle Container Registry authentication token stored in
  `~/.ocr/auth-token`, or an equivalent secure way to pass the password to
  the container tool through standard input.

- A container registry namespace if you want to push a runnable multi-platform
  tag. The main flow writes an OCI archive locally, so a registry is not
  required for the core inspection steps.

- A container build backend that can execute both `linux/amd64` and
  `linux/arm64` containers. This is required because the Dockerfile runs
  `dnf` and `jlink` while building each platform variant.

  The backend that you choose must be configured to support both platforms.
  For example, a Docker Buildx builder may provide this support directly,
  while a Podman host may need `binfmt` handlers for foreign architectures,
  such as:

  ```shell
  podman run --privileged --rm docker.io/tonistiigi/binfmt --install all
  ```

  Configure the backend that you will use before continuing, regardless of
  the operating system on which it runs.

## Build the application

The application is built once. The resulting Spring Boot JAR contains
architecture-neutral bytecode and is copied into each platform-specific image
variant. The custom Java runtime, by contrast, is created separately inside
each target-platform build.

1. Build the application.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── jlink-multi-architecture-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── jlink-multi-architecture-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

## Inspect the Dockerfile

The Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build. The builder stage starts from the
Oracle JDK image and runs `jlink`. The final stage starts from a smaller Oracle
Linux image and copies in only the custom runtime and Spring Boot JAR.

During a multi-platform build, the builder stage is evaluated for each target
platform. That means the `RUN jlink` step creates a runtime for the current
target platform variant rather than one shared runtime that is copied into
every image.

```dockerfile
FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 AS builder

WORKDIR /opt/app

ARG JAVA_MODULES=java.base,java.compiler,java.desktop,java.instrument,java.management,java.naming,java.sql,java.security.jgss

# binutils are needed by the `--strip-debug` command line option.
RUN dnf install -y binutils && dnf clean all
RUN jlink \
      --output './jre' \
      --no-header-files \
      --no-man-pages \
      --strip-debug \
      --add-modules "${JAVA_MODULES}" \
      --compress=zip-9

FROM container-registry.oracle.com/os/oraclelinux:10-slim

WORKDIR /opt/app

COPY --from=builder /opt/app/jre /opt/jre
COPY ./target/jlink-multi-architecture-spring-boot-*.jar app.jar

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["/opt/jre/bin/java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

The Dockerfile contains no explicit operating-system or architecture
conditionals. Its base-image tags resolve to the requested platform variants,
and each `RUN` instruction executes within that variant. As a result, the same
Dockerfile creates an `amd64` custom runtime for the `linux/amd64` image and an
`arm64` custom runtime for the `linux/arm64` image.

## Inspect the base image platforms

A multi-platform application image can only target platforms that are supported
by every platform-specific input it depends on. In this example, both the JDK
builder image and the Oracle Linux final-stage image need variants for the
requested platforms.

1. Inspect the Oracle Java builder image.

   ```shell
   skopeo inspect --raw 'docker://container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' | jq
   ```

   The builder image tag resolves to platform-specific image manifests.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "size": 1099,
         "digest": "sha256:06d115c14b85dc23030635780c6a587096dfb0583085c31d36be634b7efe49f2",
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "size": 1099,
         "digest": "sha256:c2fde8cea2f620b6b7dafc53fa9a4ac3f88ed41ad1ad35e085c56decdfc96d12",
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

2. Inspect the Oracle Linux final-stage image.

   ```shell
   skopeo inspect --raw 'docker://container-registry.oracle.com/os/oraclelinux:10-slim' | jq
   ```

   The final-stage image tag also resolves to platform-specific image manifests.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "digest": "sha256:5d47b9e450523400ad6c47247d1cb6f316b272091a5b6c9452f11f5be167dbdc",
         "size": 429,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "digest": "sha256:7b44e83474c0c48fea440b1495c87d3f1d6ac9e25a8c00392bcaaa60a1d91b0b",
         "size": 429,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

Both base image tags need `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` variants because those
are the two platforms requested later in this runbook.

## Build a multi-platform OCI archive

Docker Buildx and Podman can both produce a multi-platform OCI archive without
pushing to a registry. The important difference from the plain
multi-architecture example is that this Dockerfile runs `jlink` during the
build. The builder must therefore execute the `RUN jlink` step in a way that
produces a valid runtime for each requested target platform.

The Docker and Podman commands are both shown for completeness. Execute the
option that matches the environment used for the workshop. Both commands will
produce the OCI image archive and save it to
`./target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar`.

1. Build the multi-platform OCI archive.

   The `--platform` option tells the builder which operating system and CPU
   architecture combinations to build for. Here we request two Linux image
   variants: `linux/amd64` for x86-64 machines and `linux/arm64` for 64-bit ARM
   machines.

   - Using Docker.

     ```shell
     docker buildx build \
       --platform 'linux/amd64,linux/arm64' \
       --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
       --tag 'demo:jlink-multi-architecture-oci' \
       --output 'type=oci,dest=./target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' \
       .
     ```

     The `--output 'type=oci,dest=./target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar'` option
     exports the build result as an OCI image archive instead of loading it
     directly into the local image store. Because this build targets multiple
     platforms, the archive contains an OCI image index together with the
     platform-specific image manifests and layers.

   - Using Podman.

     ```shell
     podman manifest rm 'demo:jlink-multi-architecture-oci' 2>/dev/null || true

     podman build \
       --platform 'linux/amd64,linux/arm64' \
       --security-opt 'label=disable' \
       --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
       --manifest 'demo:jlink-multi-architecture-oci' \
       .

     podman manifest push \
       'demo:jlink-multi-architecture-oci' \
       'oci-archive:./target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar'
     ```

     `--manifest` names the Podman manifest list that collects the `linux/amd64`
     and `linux/arm64` images produced by this build. The subsequent
     `podman manifest push` command exports that manifest list, together with
     its platform-specific images, to the OCI archive.

     `--security-opt 'label=disable'` disables SELinux labelling for the
     temporary build containers. This allows the QEMU interpreter registered
     through `binfmt` to execute the foreign-architecture build steps on hosts
     where the default Podman SELinux label prevents it. It does not change the
     SELinux labelling of containers created from the resulting image.

   (*Optional*) Verify that the file was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name --prune -P '*.tar' './target'
   ```

   The OCI image archive should now be present under `target`.

   ```
   ./target
   └── jlink-multi-architecture.tar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

2. Inspect the OCI image index stored in the archive.

   ```shell
   IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST="$(
     tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' 'index.json' \
       | jq --raw-output '.manifests[0].digest | sub("^sha256:"; "")'
   )"

   tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' "blobs/sha256/${IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST}" | jq
   ```

   The archive contains one image manifest per requested platform.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:2797e3de1be97ec90ec0ab346a32e2b7828a9fa464a2fb9454eabe083c786d70",
         "size": 1014,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:2fdb8a7183ad2f499c05de069ad06556c8541a18fdf21e4b7d4344b76718c22e",
         "size": 1014,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   The archive’s image index contains one descriptor for each requested
   platform. Each descriptor points to a separate image manifest, and each image
   manifest references the layers for that platform’s final image. Because
   `jlink` ran during the build, the custom runtime copied into the final image
   is part of the platform-specific result.

3. Compare the platform-specific image manifest descriptors.

   ```shell
   IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST="$(
     tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' 'index.json' \
       | jq --raw-output '.manifests[0].digest | sub("^sha256:"; "")'
   )"

   tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' "blobs/sha256/${IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST}" | jq
   ```

   Each platform descriptor has its own image manifest digest.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:2797e3de1be97ec90ec0ab346a32e2b7828a9fa464a2fb9454eabe083c786d70",
         "size": 1014,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:2fdb8a7183ad2f499c05de069ad06556c8541a18fdf21e4b7d4344b76718c22e",
         "size": 1014,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   Different manifest digests are expected. These descriptors do not show the
   layer contents directly, but they do prove that the archive contains separate
   image manifests for the requested platforms. The application JAR is shared
   input, while the custom runtime and base-image layers are platform-specific.
   Do not build a `jlink` runtime once on one architecture and copy it into
   every platform variant.
